name: Michaelis-Menten Kinetics
statement: An enzyme's rate rises with substrate, then levels off as the enzyme saturates.
statementAccent: then levels off as the enzyme saturates
meaning: Michaelis-Menten kinetics is the standard model of how the speed of an enzyme-catalysed reaction depends on the amount of substrate. At low substrate the rate climbs almost in proportion, but as substrate increases the enzyme becomes saturated and the rate flattens toward a maximum. The relationship is a rectangular hyperbola, summarised by two numbers: the maximum rate and the substrate concentration that gives half of it, called the Michaelis constant.
mechanism: The enzyme binds substrate to form a complex that then breaks down into product, freeing the enzyme. When substrate is scarce, most enzyme is idle and adding more substrate speeds things up; when substrate is plentiful, nearly all the enzyme is occupied and the rate is limited by how fast the complex turns over, giving the maximum rate. The Michaelis constant is the substrate concentration at half-maximum rate; under a rapid-equilibrium assumption it reflects binding affinity, but in the more general steady-state treatment it also folds in the catalytic step.

examples.text: Plotting rate against substrate gives a curve that rises steeply then plateaus, the hallmark shape of an enzyme approaching its maximum turnover.

The ratio of the turnover number to the Michaelis constant, the catalytic efficiency, lets biochemists compare how effectively different enzymes convert substrate, especially when substrate is scarce.
Pharmacologists use the model to describe how quickly enzymes clear a drug and how that rate saturates at higher doses.

variants.name: The Briggs-Haldane steady state
variants.text: The 1925 refinement that derives the equation by assuming the enzyme-substrate complex holds a nearly constant level, the basis of most modern textbook treatments.

variants.name: Cooperative enzymes
variants.text: Allosteric enzymes give a sigmoidal, S-shaped curve rather than a hyperbola, described by the Hill equation, and fall outside the simple Michaelis-Menten model.

whyItMatters: It is the foundational framework of enzyme kinetics, giving biochemists a common language of maximum rate, Michaelis constant, turnover number, and catalytic efficiency to characterise and compare enzymes. Its steady-state logic extends to transporters, receptors, and drug metabolism, making it central to enzymology and pharmacology and one of the most widely used quantitative models in the life sciences.

working.text: characterise an enzyme by its maximum rate and its Michaelis constant, the substrate level at half-maximum rate.
apply the model to early-reaction rates under steady state, with substrate in large excess and before product builds up.
switch to a cooperative model when the rate curve is sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic, since Michaelis-Menten will not fit.

limits: It is a well-established but simplifying model, assuming a single substrate, steady-state or rapid-equilibrium conditions, no product inhibition, and substrate in large excess over enzyme. It does not describe allosteric or cooperative enzymes, whose curves are sigmoidal, nor multi-substrate reactions without extension, nor fast pre-steady-state transients. The Michaelis constant equals the dissociation constant only under the rapid-equilibrium assumption; in general it also includes the catalytic rate, so it is an apparent affinity rather than a pure binding constant.
misreadings: The Michaelis constant is not exactly the enzyme-substrate binding affinity; that holds only under rapid equilibrium, and in the general steady-state treatment it also contains the catalytic step, making it an apparent affinity. The model is not universal; cooperative and multi-substrate enzymes need different equations. And the maximum rate is not an intrinsic constant of the enzyme alone but depends on how much enzyme is present.
origin: Introduced by Leonor Michaelis and Maud Menten in 1913, building on Victor Henri's 1903 work, and given its modern steady-state derivation by George Briggs and J. B. S. Haldane in 1925.

sources.text: Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Wikipedia. — the rate equation, the two parameters, the Henri and Briggs-Haldane history, and the assumptions.
